content: Al Herpin was famously known as The Man Who Never Slept. He was born in 1853 in Trenton, New Jersey, and claimed to have a rare form of insomnia that rendered him incapable of sleeping. The exact cause of his condition remains unknown, though it has been speculated that it might be related to a significant injury his mother suffered just days before his birth. In the late 1940s, Al Herpin's extraordinary claim drew the attention of medical professionals, who visited his home to investigate. They discovered that he did not own a bed or any furniture typically associated with sleep. Instead, he had only a rocking chair. Herpin explained that after a long day of work, he would sit in his rocking chair, read the newspaper until dawn, and then return to work. Despite his lack of sleep, he was reportedly in excellent health and maintained a high level of alertness, challenging the scientific understanding of the necessity of sleep. A report in The New York Times on February 29, 1904, stated that Albert Herpin, who was born in France in 1862 and had worked for 15 years as a hostler for Freeholder Walter Phares, claimed he had not slept at all for the past ten years. Remarkably, he appeared to be in perfect health and did not seem to experience any discomfort from his unusual condition. Al Herpin passed away on January 3, 1947, at the age of 94. His death prompted another article in The New York Times, which expressed skepticism about his claims. The article described him as a recluse who lived on the outskirts of the city and insisted that he never slept. When questioned about his sleeplessness, Herpin maintained that he never truly dozed off but merely rested. No other individual with complete insomnia has been documented to live for such an extended period. It is believed that his death was due to causes unrelated to sleep deprivation, as his insomnia did not appear to have negatively impacted his health.
